objectives: Connect fusion + advanced fission to future grids.

slides.title: Fusion: the other side of the binding-energy curve
slides.body:
Fusion releases energy by combining light nuclei toward Fe-56. The most practical reaction:

  **D + T → ⁴He (3.5 MeV) + n (14.1 MeV) + 17.6 MeV**

• Deuterium: 0.015% of natural hydrogen. Abundant (oceans contain ~10¹⁴ tonnes).
• Tritium: not naturally abundant. Made by neutron capture on Li-6: n + ⁶Li → ³H + ⁴He.
• Lithium: abundant in seawater + crustal rock.

Fusion power density (per unit mass of fuel): ~3-4× higher than fission per unit mass; per unit volume in a reactor, similar order.

**Advantages vs fission**:
• No long-lived high-level waste (only short-lived activation of structural materials).
• No proliferation pathway (no fissile material).
• Inherent passive safety (cannot 'runaway' — needs continuous external heating).
• Abundant fuel.
• Lower carbon footprint.

**Challenges**:
• Plasma at 100M+ degrees C — hotter than the Sun's core.
• Confinement: gravity (stars), magnetic (tokamak), inertial (laser fusion).
• **Lawson criterion**: nτT > critical value (where n = density, τ = confinement time, T = temperature). For D-T at ~150 keV: n·τ > 10²⁰ s/m³.

Decades of research; multi-billion-dollar machines (JET, ITER, NIF, etc.). 2022: NIF achieved 'scientific breakeven' (3.15 MJ output vs 2.05 MJ laser input — ignoring electricity inefficiency upstream).

slides.title: Magnetic confinement fusion: tokamaks + stellarators
slides.body:
**Tokamak** (toroidal chamber): plasma confined in a torus by helical magnetic field. Toroidal field from external coils + poloidal field from a plasma current induced by transformer. ~150 million °C, ~10²⁰ m⁻³ density, ~1 s confinement.

Key experiments:
• **JET (Joint European Torus, UK)**: 1983-2023. Largest tokamak; record fusion power (16 MW in 1997; 59 MJ total in 2021). Decommissioning.
• **JT-60SA (Japan)**: 2023 first plasma; bridge to ITER.
• **EAST (China)**: long-duration plasma demos.
• **KSTAR (Korea)**: long-duration high-confinement.
• **DIII-D, NSTX (US)**: research.
• **SPARC (US, Commonwealth Fusion Systems)**: HTS magnet pioneer, planned 2025-26.
• **ITER (France, international)**: 35-country project; 500 MW fusion target; first plasma ~2034 (delayed); D-T operation ~2039. €20+B cost. Goal: demonstrate net energy Q = 10 (500 MW fusion vs 50 MW heating input).
• **STEP (UK)**: stellarator + tokamak; commercial design.
• **Commonwealth Fusion (SPARC + ARC)**: HTS magnet-enabled compact tokamak; 2025-2030 demonstration.
• **Tokamak Energy (UK)**: spherical tokamak.

**Stellarator** alternative geometry: helical-coil twist replaces plasma current. Stable (no disruption risk), but harder to design.
• **W7-X (Germany)**: largest operating stellarator; record 60-min plasma 2023.
• **HSX (US)**: research.

**Plasma physics challenges**:
- **Disruptions**: tokamak plasma can suddenly collapse (a quenched plasma current spike). Mitigated by injected gas, killer pellets, ML-based prediction.
- **Plasma-facing materials**: must survive 14 MeV neutrons + plasma heat. Tungsten + advanced steels (RAFM, ODS); 50+ year lifetime hard.
- **Tritium breeding**: Li blankets generate T from neutron capture. Tritium self-sufficiency needed (no global T supply for commercial fleet).
- **Heating + current drive**: ICRH, NBI, ECH — combination of methods to maintain plasma.
- **Divertor**: removes He 'ash' + heat exhaust. Concentrated heat flux (~10 MW/m²) on divertor target; major engineering challenge.

slides.title: Inertial confinement fusion + Q-physics
slides.body:
**Inertial confinement fusion (ICF)**: tiny D-T pellet (~1 mm) compressed by laser/X-ray drive; fuel ignites + burns before plasma flies apart (~ns timescale).

• **NIF (Lawrence Livermore)**: 192 laser beams, 2.05 MJ on target.
• **2022 milestone**: 3.15 MJ fusion energy from 2.05 MJ laser input — first 'scientific breakeven' (target Q > 1). Sparked global excitement.
• **Engineering breakeven (Q_total > 1)**: laser plug-to-target efficiency ~1% — facility consumed ~300 MJ from grid to deliver 2 MJ on target. So total Q > 1 requires ~150× more progress.
• **Commercial breakeven**: factor 50-100 more output, sustained, with target rep rate 10+ Hz, target fabrication at ~$0.10 per pellet. Still very far away.

**Other ICF approaches**:
- **Z-pinch** (Sandia Z-machine): magnetic compression by pulsed current.
- **Direct-drive**: laser hits pellet directly (LLE Omega).
- **Indirect-drive**: laser hits hohlraum to produce X-rays which drive pellet (NIF).
- **Magnetized target fusion** (General Fusion): liquid metal compression of magnetized plasma.
- **Fast ignition** (research): separate compression + ignition phases.

**Other private fusion companies (2024)**:
- **Helion**: Field-Reversed Configuration (FRC); D-He³ fuel; aiming D-He³ commercial 2028.
- **TAE Technologies**: FRC + advanced beam-driven; aiming p-B11 (no neutrons) eventually.
- **Zap Energy**: sheared-flow Z-pinch.
- **Marvel Fusion**: lasers + nanostructured targets.
- **Pacific Fusion, Realta, Avalanche, others**

**Status (2024)**:
- Scientific breakeven demonstrated in ICF (NIF 2022); engineering net energy still far.
- Magnetic confinement: ITER will be the deciding experiment for next-gen design choices.
- Commercial timeline: optimistic 2035-2045; realistic 2050-2070.
- Private investment surge ($6B+ to fusion startups by 2024) accelerating but skeptics remain.

**Why fusion is hard**: the physics is well-understood; the engineering is brutal. Materials, tritium breeding, plasma control, economics, supply chain — each a generation of engineering work. Comparable in difficulty to commercial aviation circa 1920 — fundamentals were known, decades of refinement needed.

question.question: Compute the energy density of D-T fusion + compare to fission
question.goal: D-T fusion: 17.6 MeV per reaction. Reactants: 1 D nucleus + 1 T nucleus (atomic masses ~2 + ~3 amu). Compare to U-235 fission (200 MeV per reaction, ~235 amu).

steps.prompt: Energy per amu for D-T fusion?
steps.reveal: Fusion energy density: 17.6 MeV / 5 amu = 3.52 MeV/amu. ~3.4× higher than fission's 200/235 ≈ 0.85 MeV/amu per nucleon mass.

steps.prompt: Energy per kg of D-T fuel?
hints: 3.5 MeV/amu × 6×10²³ amu/g × 1000 g/kg = 2.1×10²⁷ MeV/kg = 3.36×10¹⁴ J/kg. Same as 94 GWh/kg.
steps.reveal: ~3.4×10¹⁴ J/kg ≈ 94 GWh/kg thermal. About 4× more than U-235 fission (82 TJ/kg thermal = 23 GWh/kg).

steps.prompt: Per kg of fuel, how does fusion compare to oil (44 MJ/kg)?
steps.reveal: Fusion is ~8 million times more energy-dense per kg than oil. If commercial fusion is realized, fuel scarcity is essentially eliminated — D and Li are abundant in seawater + crust.

steps.prompt: Why isn't fusion already powering the grid then?

acceptedAnswers: plasma containment + Lawson criterion + materials + tritium breeding + economics

steps.reveal: Multiple compounding challenges: (1) plasma at 150M °C — hotter than the Sun; (2) Lawson criterion nτT > 10²⁰ keV·s/m³ — combination hard to simultaneously achieve; (3) materials must survive 14 MeV neutron bombardment for years; (4) tritium breeding self-sufficient; (5) divertor handling 10+ MW/m² heat flux; (6) economics — capex ~$10-30B per gigawatt-class plant, electricity cost competitive with cheap solar+wind+storage; (7) supply chain for HTS magnets, plasma-facing components, tritium handling. Each is a 20-30 yr engineering challenge. ITER will answer some; commercial fusion 2035-2070 horizon depending on optimism.

question.question: Why did the NIF 2022 'scientific breakeven' announcement not mean commercial fusion is imminent?
options: NIF achieved Q_scientific = output_fusion / energy_into_target ≈ 1.5 (3.15 MJ fusion vs 2.05 MJ laser energy on target). But the lasers themselves are ~1% efficient — facility drew ~300 MJ from the grid to deliver 2 MJ. So Q_engineering ≈ 0.01. Plus: NIF fires once every ~few hours (not 10 Hz for commercial), uses expensive cryogenic D-T pellets, doesn't breed tritium, doesn't extract heat as electricity. Real engineering breakeven would need 100-1000× current laser efficiency × repetition rate × target fabrication economics × tritium-breeding + thermal-to-electric conversion. Demonstrates physics, not engineering economics.
Inertial confinement has been commercial since 1990.
question.explanation:
**NIF 2022 milestone**: 192 laser beams delivered 2.05 MJ of energy to a D-T pellet; fusion reactions produced 3.15 MJ. Q_scientific = 3.15/2.05 ≈ 1.54.

This was the first demonstration ever of *target* gain (more energy out than into the target itself). Major physics achievement; National Academy of Engineering Lawrence Award; major fusion-energy-research milestone.

**Why not commercial**:

1. **Laser efficiency** ~1%: NIF lasers are flashlamp-pumped Nd:glass amplifiers. Wall-plug electricity → laser energy on target conversion is poor. ~300 MJ drawn from grid for 2 MJ on target. → Q_engineering = 3.15/300 ≈ 0.01. Modern diode-pumped lasers can achieve ~10-20% efficiency — would improve by ~10-20×. Still not 100× needed.

2. **Repetition rate**: NIF fires at most once every ~few hours (laser cooling, target setup). Commercial fusion needs ~10 Hz (10 shots/second). Need to develop new laser architectures + target injection systems.

3. **Target cost**: NIF targets cost ~$millions each (cryogenic D-T pellets in special holohraums, hand-fabricated). Commercial would need ~$0.10/target with mass production.

4. **Tritium**: NIF uses ~µg of T per shot. Commercial plant needs ~50 kg/yr T. T must be bred from Li in blanket — not demonstrated at scale.

5. **Heat extraction + electricity**: NIF dumps heat into water; commercial plant needs to extract + convert to electricity (steam cycle ~33%, or higher with Brayton). Add ~50-70% loss.

6. **Containment + materials**: 14-MeV neutron flux damages structural materials. Replacing first-wall on a power-plant schedule (yrs-decades) is required.

7. **Economics**: even if all of (1)-(6) solved, capital cost ($10-30B/GW) + cost of electricity ($/MWh) must compete with cheap solar+wind+storage ($25-40/MWh) — very hard.

**ICF vs MCF for commercial**:
- MCF (tokamaks) more mature for continuous power generation; ITER will be the deciding experiment.
- ICF (NIF + private) may find niches (compact, modular, military spinoffs).
- Hybrid + advanced concepts (magnetized target, fast ignition) also pursued.

**Realistic timeline**:
- Demonstration plant: 2035-2045
- First commercial reactor: 2050-2070
- Significant grid penetration: 2070-2100

**Optimists**: SPARC, ITER, Helion, NIF could compress this timeline. Commonwealth Fusion targets 2030s demo.

**Skeptics**: Decades of unmet promises; engineering challenges underestimated. Solar+wind+storage already meeting decarbonization needs.

Fusion is real, important, + happening — but commercial timescale remains genuinely decades away. NIF 2022 was a physics milestone, not an engineering one.

slides.workedSolution: NIF Q_scientific = 1.54 (3.15 MJ fusion / 2.05 MJ to target). BUT: laser efficiency ~1%, so 300 MJ from grid for 2 MJ to target → Q_engineering ≈ 0.01. Commercial needs: laser efficiency 20-30%, rep rate 10 Hz (vs once per few hours), target cost $0.10 vs $millions, tritium breeding in Li blanket, heat-to-electricity conversion, materials surviving 14-MeV neutrons, capital cost competitive with solar+storage. Realistic commercial fusion: 2050-2070.

question.question: How does fusion compare to advanced fission (Gen IV) for decarbonization timing?
options: Advanced fission (Gen IV, including SMRs + sodium-fast reactors + MSRs) has multiple demonstrators operating (BN-800 Russia, HTR-PM China, TMSR-LF1 China) + commercial deployment 2025-2035 horizon. Fusion has scientific breakeven (NIF 2022) but no commercial demo + commercial timeline 2050-2070. For decarbonization by 2050 (Paris Agreement targets), advanced fission is the realistic nuclear contribution; fusion's role is later 21st century. Both important; deployment timing differs by ~20-40 years.
Fission is obsolete; only fusion matters.
question.explanation:
**Fusion vs advanced fission timing comparison**:

**Advanced fission (Gen IV + SMR)**:
- BN-800 Russia: operational since 2016 (sodium-cooled fast reactor).
- HTR-PM China: operational since 2023 (gas-cooled HTGR).
- TMSR-LF1 China: first criticality 2023 (molten salt thorium).
- BWRX-300 (Canada, US): construction starting 2024-25 (commercial).
- NuScale: licensed 2020 (US); CFPP canceled 2023 over cost; other projects ongoing.
- TerraPower Natrium: Wyoming construction 2024-2030.
- X-energy: TRISO HTGR commercial 2028-2030.
- Rolls-Royce SMR: UK construction late 2020s.
- Multiple Gen IV demos operating; commercial deployment in 2025-2035 horizon.

**Fusion**:
- NIF 2022: scientific breakeven (Q_sci > 1) — physics milestone.
- ITER: first plasma 2034 (delayed); full D-T operation 2039. Goal Q = 10 demonstration.
- SPARC (CFS): aiming Q > 2 by 2026-27 (HTS magnet-enabled compact).
- DEMO (post-ITER): 2050s commercial demo plant.
- First commercial fusion plant: 2050-2070 realistic.

**For 2050 decarbonization target**:
- Advanced fission can contribute meaningfully (10-30% of new low-carbon generation by 2050).
- Fusion's role: very small or zero by 2050; meaningful contribution 2070+.
- Solar + wind + storage will dominate the bulk of 2050 grid in most regions.
- Existing LWR fleet: ~5-10% of global generation through 2060+ (life extensions).

**Why both are needed**:
- Fission: meets near-term decarbonization (2020-2050).
- Fusion: meets long-term sustainable energy supply (2050-2100+).
- Different physics, different infrastructure, different timelines.
- Fusion's promise (no proliferation, no high-level waste, abundant fuel) is real but the realization is 20-40 yr later than fission.

**Common talking-point error**: 'Fusion is just 20 years away' has been said for 50+ years. It's *also* probably true now — but 'just' means 20-50 years, not by 2030.

**Investment outlook (2024)**:
- Fusion: $6B+ in private companies (Commonwealth, Helion, TAE, etc.) + ~$2B/yr public (ITER, NIF, etc.)
- Advanced fission + SMR: $20B+ committed in IRA, EU, UK, Korea, Japan, China + commercial orders.
- Renewables: $1.7T/yr (2023 IEA).

Decarbonization will use all of them. The question isn't fission vs fusion vs renewables — it's how to deploy each at the right time at the right scale.

slides.workedSolution: Advanced fission (Gen IV + SMR): demos operating (BN-800, HTR-PM, TMSR-LF1); commercial 2025-2035 horizon (BWRX, Natrium, X-energy). Fusion: NIF scientific breakeven 2022 (physics); ITER 2039 D-T (research); commercial 2050-2070. For 2050 decarbonization: fission meaningful contribution, fusion likely zero. Solar+wind+storage dominate bulk. Both nuclear technologies needed but at different timescales — fission for 2020-2050, fusion for 2050-2100+. Common error: 'fusion 20 yr away for 50 yr' — also true now, but 'just' means 20-50 yr, not 2030.

question.question: D-T fusion releases 17.6 MeV per reaction. How many reactions per second are needed to produce 1 GW thermal power?
question.hint: P = N × E_per_reaction. N = P/E = 10⁹ W / (17.6 MeV × 1.6×10⁻¹³ J/MeV) = 10⁹ / 2.82×10⁻¹² = 3.55×10²⁰ /s.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain to a sustainability policymaker the realistic role of fusion in the 21st-century energy transition.
question.rubric: Mentions: fusion's promise — abundant fuel (D + Li), no long-lived waste, no proliferation, inherently safe (passive), high energy density. But commercial timeline 2050-2070+ realistic; ITER full D-T 2039; first commercial plant 2050s at earliest. Decarbonization to meet 2050 net-zero targets must rely on: solar + wind + storage (dominant new generation), existing LWR fleet (life extensions), advanced fission (Gen IV, SMRs) for new dispatchable baseload, demand-side measures + efficiency. Fusion's role: late 21st century. Investment now (~$8-10B/yr public + private) is appropriate — pays off long-term + has spinoff benefits (materials science, plasma physics, HTS magnets used elsewhere). Concludes: fusion ≠ silver bullet for 2050; it's the next-generation energy supply for 2050-2100+. Both fission + fusion needed; both have specific roles + timelines. Pretending fusion is imminent misallocates urgency.
